{{short description|Famous saying by Socrates}}
{{Socrates}}
"'''I know that I know nothing'''" is a saying derived from [[Plato]]'s account of the [[Classical Greece|Greek]] [[philosopher]] [[Socrates]]: ''"For I was conscious that I knew practically nothing..."'' ([[Plato]], Apology 22d, translated by Harold North Fowler, 1966).<ref>[https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.01.0169%3Atext%3DApol.%3Asection%3D22d Plato. Plato in Twelve Volumes, Vol. 1 translated by Harold North Fowler; Introduction by W.R.M. Lamb. Cambridge, MA, Harvard University Press; London, William Heinemann Ltd. 1966.]</ref> It is also sometimes called the '''Socratic paradox''', although this name is often instead used to refer to other seemingly paradoxical claims made by [[Socrates]] in [[Plato]]'s dialogues (most notably, [[Socratic intellectualism]] and the Socratic fallacy).<ref>{{cite web |title=Socratic Paradox |url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/view/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803100515858 |website=Oxford Reference |access-date=19 November 2021}}</ref>

This saying is also connected or conflated with the [[List of oracular statements from Delphi#440 BC|answer]] to a question [[Socrates]] (according to [[Xenophon]]) or [[Chaerephon]] (according to [[Plato]]) is said to have posed to the [[Pythia]], the [[Oracle of Delphi]], in which the oracle stated something to the effect of "Socrates is the wisest person in [[Athens]]."<ref>H. Bowden, ''Classical Athens and the Delphic Oracle: Divination and Democracy'', Cambridge University Press, 2005, [https://archive.org/details/classicalathensd0000bowd/page/82 <!-- quote=Chaerophon asked the Oracle. --> p. 82].</ref> [[Socrates]], believing the oracle but also completely convinced that he knew nothing, was said to have concluded that ''nobody'' knew anything, and that he was only wiser than others because he was the only person who recognized his own ignorance.

== Etymology ==
The phrase, originally<!--see talk page section: "Original Greek"--> from [[Latin]] ("''{{lang|la|ipse se nihil scire id unum sciat}}''"),<ref>"He himself thinks he knows one thing, that he knows nothing"; [[Cicero]], ''Academica'', [https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A2007.01.0032%3Abook%3D1%3Asection%3D16 Book I, section 16].</ref> is a possible paraphrase from a [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] text (see below). It is also quoted as "''{{lang|la|scio me nihil scire}}''" or "''{{lang|la|scio me nescire}}''".<ref>A variant is found in [[Nicholas of Cusa|von Kues]], ''De visione Dei'', XIII, 146 (''Werke'', Walter de Gruyter, 1967, p. 312): "''...et hoc scio solum, quia scio me nescire {{sic}}...'' [I know alone, that (''or'' because) I know, that I do not know]."</ref> It was later [[Back-translation|back-translated]]<!--see talk page section: "Original Greek"--> to [[Katharevousa Greek]] as "{{lang|grc|[ἓν οἶδα ὅτι] οὐδὲν οἶδα}}" ([''hèn oîda hóti''] ''oudèn oîda'').<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.translatum.gr/forum/index.php?topic=918.0|title=All I know is that I know nothing -> Ἓν οἶδα ὅτι οὐδὲν οἶδα, Εν οίδα ότι ουδέν οίδα, ΕΝ ΟΙΔΑ ΟΤΙ ΟΥΔΕΝ ΟΙΔΑ|website=www.translatum.gr}}</ref>

== In Plato ==
This is technically a shorter paraphrasing of [[Socrates]]' statement, "I neither know nor think I know" (in [[Plato]], ''Apology'' 21d). The paraphrased saying, though widely attributed to [[Plato]]'s Socrates in both ancient and modern times, actually occurs nowhere in [[Plato]]'s works in precisely the form "I know I know nothing."<ref>Gail Fine, "Does Socrates Claim to Know that He Knows Nothing?", ''Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy'' vol. 35 (2008), pp. 49–88.</ref>  As of 2008, two prominent [[Plato]] scholars had argued that the claim should not be attributed to [[Plato]]'s Socrates.<ref>Fine argues that "it is better not to attribute it to him" ("Does Socrates Claim to Know He Knows Nothing?", ''Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy'' vol. 35 (2008), p. 51). C. C. W. Taylor has argued that the "paradoxical formulation is a clear misreading of Plato" (''Socrates'', Oxford University Press 1998, p. 46).</ref>

Evidence that [[Socrates]] does not actually claim to know nothing can be found at ''Apology'' 29b-c, where he claims twice to know something. See also ''Apology'' 29d, where [[Socrates]] indicates that he is so confident in his claim to knowledge at 29b-c that he is willing to die for it.{{cn|date=March 2023}}

That said, in the ''[[Apology (Plato)|Apology]]'', [[Plato]] relates that [[Socrates]] accounts for his seeming wiser than any other person because he does not imagine that he knows what he does not know.<ref name="auto">Plato, ''Apology'' 21d.</ref>

<blockquote>
{{lang|grc|... ἔοικα γοῦν τούτου γε σμικρῷ τινι αὐτῷ τούτῳ σοφώτερος εἶναι, ὅτι ἃ μὴ οἶδα οὐδὲ οἴομαι εἰδέναι.}}
<br>... I seem, then, in just this little thing to be wiser than this man at any rate, that what I do not know I do not think I know either. [Henry Cary literal translation of 1897]
</blockquote>

A more commonly used translation puts it, <blockquote>Although I do not suppose that either of us knows anything really beautiful and good, I am better off than he is – for he knows nothing, and thinks he knows. I neither know nor think I know. [<nowiki/>[[Benjamin Jowett]] translation].</blockquote>Regardless, the context in which this passage occurs is the same, independently of any specific translation. That is, [[Socrates]] having gone to a "wise" man, and having discussed with him, withdraws and thinks the above to himself. [[Socrates]], since he denied any kind of knowledge, then tried to find someone wiser than himself among politicians, poets, and craftsmen. It appeared that politicians claimed wisdom without knowledge; poets could touch people with their words, but did not know their meaning; and craftsmen could claim knowledge only in specific and narrow fields. The interpretation of the Oracle's answer might be [[Socrates]]' awareness of his own ignorance.<ref name="PlatoKaplan2009">{{cite book|author1=Plato|author2=Morris Kaplan|title=The Socratic Dialogues|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SSous9E-3CwC&pg=PR9|date=2009|publisher=Kaplan Publishing|isbn=978-1-4277-9953-1|page=9}}</ref>  

[[Socrates]] also deals with this phrase in [[Plato]]'s dialogue ''[[Meno]]'' when he says:<ref>Plato, ''Meno'' 80d1–3.</ref>

<blockquote>
{{lang|grc|καὶ νῦν περὶ ἀρετῆς ὃ ἔστιν ἐγὼ μὲν οὐκ οἶδα, σὺ μέντοι ἴσως πρότερον μὲν ᾔδησθα πρὶν ἐμοῦ ἅψασθαι, νῦν μέντοι ὅμοιος εἶ οὐκ εἰδότι.}}

So now I do not know what virtue is; perhaps you knew before you contacted me, but now you are certainly like one who does not know. ([[George Grube|G. M. A. Grube]] translation)
</blockquote>

Here, [[Socrates]] aims at the change of Meno's opinion, who was a firm believer in his own opinion and whose claim to knowledge [[Socrates]] had disproved.

It is essentially the question that begins "[[Pre-Socratic|post-Socratic]]" Western philosophy. Socrates begins all wisdom with wondering, thus one must begin with admitting one's ignorance. After all, Socrates' dialectic method of teaching was based on that he as a teacher knew nothing, so he would derive knowledge from his students by dialogue.

There is also a passage by [[Diogenes Laërtius]] in his work ''[[Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers]]'' written hundreds of years after [[Plato]], where he lists, among the things that Socrates used to say:<ref>Diogenes Laërtius II.32.</ref> "{{lang|grc|εἰδέναι μὲν μηδὲν πλὴν αὐτὸ τοῦτο εἰδέναι}}", or "that he knew nothing except that he knew that very fact (i.e. that he knew nothing)".

Again, closer to the quote, there is a passage in [[Plato]]'s ''Apology'', where Socrates says that after discussing with someone he started thinking that:<ref name="auto"/>

<blockquote>
{{lang|grc|τούτου μὲν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐγὼ σοφώτερός εἰμι· κινδυνεύει μὲν γὰρ ἡμῶν οὐδέτερος οὐδὲν καλὸν κἀγαθὸν εἰδέναι, ἀλλ᾽ οὗτος μὲν οἴεταί τι εἰδέναι οὐκ εἰδώς, ἐγὼ δέ, ὥσπερ οὖν οὐκ οἶδα, οὐδὲ οἴομαι· ἔοικα γοῦν τούτου γε σμικρῷ τινι αὐτῷ τούτῳ σοφώτερος εἶναι, ὅτι ἃ μὴ οἶδα οὐδὲ οἴομαι εἰδέναι.}}

I am wiser than this man, for neither of us appears to know anything great and good; but he fancies he knows something, although he knows nothing; whereas I, as I do not know anything, do not fancy I do. In this trifling particular, then, I appear to be wiser than he, because I do not fancy I know what I do not know.
</blockquote>

It is also a curiosity that there is more than one passage in the narratives in which Socrates claims to have knowledge on some topic, for instance on love:<ref>Cimakasky, Joseph J. [https://dsc.duq.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1067&context=etd All of a Sudden: The Role of Ἐξαίφνης in Plato's Dialogues]. Doctor of Philosophy Dissertation. Duquesne University. 2014.</ref>

<blockquote>
How could I vote 'No,' when the only thing I know is the art of love? (τὰ ἐρωτικά)<ref>[[Plato]]. [https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.01.0174%3Atext%3DSym.%3Asection%3D177 ''Symposium'', 177d-e].</ref>

I know virtually nothing, except a certain small subject – love (τῶν ἐρωτικῶν), although on this subject, I'm thought to be amazing (δεινός), better than anyone else, past or present.<ref>[[Plato]]. [https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.01.0176%3Atext%3DTheag.%3Asection%3D128b ''Theages'', 128b].</ref>
</blockquote>

== Alternative usage ==
"[[Socratic paradox (disambiguation)|Socratic paradox]]" may also refer to statements of Socrates that seem contrary to common sense, such as that "no one desires evil".<ref>[[Terence Irwin]], ''The Development of Ethics'', vol. 1, Oxford University Press 2007, p. 14; Gerasimos Santas, "The Socratic Paradoxes", ''Philosophical Review'' 73 (1964), pp. 147–64.</ref>

The words of the [[apostle St. Paul]] are also found paralleling this saying in {{Bibleverse|1Cor|8:2}}, "''Anyone who claims to know something does not yet have the necessary knowledge.''"<ref>{{Cite web |title=1 Corinthians 8:2: Commentaries |url=https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/8-2.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240521063405/https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/8-2.htm |archive-date=21 May 2024 |website=Bible Hub |quote=The Enchiridion of Epictetus supplies a [parallel] to 1 Corinthians 8:2 : “Prefer to seem to know nothing; and if to any thou shouldst seem to be somebody, distrust thyself”; similarly Socrates, in Plato’s Apology, 23.}}</ref>
